scenario: The support quality lead is the accuracy owner and a self-service product lead is the coverage owner. The roles differ after punctuation, parenthetical suffixes and case are normalised.

The accuracy owner can require the surface to abstain on the returns question class without the coverage owner's agreement. The coverage owner's job is to fix the inputs and retrieval for that class so it can be answered again within the bar.
The owners disagree about a question class. The head of customer operations decides within five days, and the accuracy owner's abstention requirement stays in force until that decision.
A chief of staff who is neither owner reviews the split every 90 days, with the next review date recorded in the future.

A new colleague finds the scope and refusal rule, the input list with acknowledgement dates, the budget with its sample size, and the name the alert reaches. Each takes under a minute and the result is recorded as a four-item checklist.
Both owners are specific on-call functions with different names, one for accuracy and one for coverage of the order-support surface.
The self-service lead is named as both accuracy owner and coverage owner, so the role rewarded for coverage also controls the error rate.
The accuracy owner is recorded as 'Support quality lead' and the coverage owner as 'Support quality lead (support)', which are the same role once the parenthetical suffix is removed.
The accuracy owner may file an opinion about an unsafe question class, but only the coverage owner can decide whether the surface abstains on it.
The coverage owner is allowed to override an abstention requirement they disagree with, turning the split into a veto held by the coverage side.
The accuracy owner is recorded as the customer support team, with no person or specific on-call function accountable for the error rate.
After recording the split, the analyst directly changes the production abstention rule for the returns question class without an operator applying it.
The one-minute retrieval test is a paragraph saying everything is on the wiki, with no timing, and the alert recipient turns out to take ten minutes to find.
